attribution.note: Marcus wrote this in his own post, reporting a study's findings in his own words.

semantics.note: Keeps both figures, the ~30-step qualifier and the memory-augmented scope, and frames them as the new study's findings.

contract.note: An ordinary reading: the claim holds if the study reported these figures. Accepting a reputable report is reasonable because the paper could not be found.

evidence.note: ISMG, May 8, 2026, quotes a lead author. It reports 94% poisoning among memory-retaining agents and nearly 90% drift after roughly 30 steps, which fits 89.4%.

Wallstreetcn, May 6, gives the exact 89.4% and 94% figures. It may partly echo Marcus, but it adds paper details beyond his post. Its separate 67%-at-15-steps figure measures something else and is no conflict.

reviews.rationale: Two reports that predate the cutoff give both figures as the study's findings. One of them, ISMG, quotes a lead author. The 67% figure is drift at 15 steps, not 30, so it does not contradict the claim. The primary paper is unavailable, but the contract accepts reliable reports.

semantics.note: Faithful. It keeps the sample of 847 deployments, the 91% rate and the framing that this is what the study found. The list of institutions is left out of the proposition but kept in the contract.

contract.note: Fair. It is scored on what the study reported, not on whether 91% of all real-world agents are vulnerable.

evidence.note: ISMG confirms the institutions, the 847 deployments and the four sectors. Its 'software development' matches code-generation.

Wallstreetcn gives the same 847 and 91% figures plus a sector breakdown. It may partly draw on Marcus.

reviews.rationale: Reports dated before the cutoff, one of which quotes a lead author, confirm the institutions, the 847 deployments, the four sectors and the 91% tool-chaining rate. No report gives conflicting figures.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: Faithful. The proposition says 'reinforce' for 'amplifies', and the February timing and AWS/Berkeley authorship are kept.

contract.note: Counting the February 2026 v2 revision as 'February' is lenient, since STAC first appeared in Sept 2025. ISMG independently calls it a February paper, and the core claim about similar vulnerabilities holds either way.

evidence.note: STAC v2, revised Feb 2, 2026. It reports that agents are highly vulnerable to tool-chaining attacks, with attack success above 90% in most cases.
v3, July 2026, before the cutoff. Used only for affiliations: UC Berkeley and AWS AI Labs.
ISMG links the new study to the February AWS/UC Berkeley paper and says both describe the same tool-chaining dynamic.

reviews.rationale: An AWS AI Labs and UC Berkeley paper, revised February 2026, documented tool-chaining vulnerabilities similar to the new study's 91% finding. ISMG draws the same link. One caveat: the paper first appeared in Sept 2025, so 'February' refers to its revision.
